Article Title: 'That hurts us': CWG silver medalist Lovlina flags 'missing' Northeast on Glasgow restaurant's India map
Article Text:
CWG silver medallist Lovlina objects to 'missing' Northeast on Glasgow restaurant's napkins (Image/PTI,X)

NEW DELHI: Commonwealth Games silver medallist and Assam boxer Lovlina Borgohain said she felt 'hurt' after noticing that the Northeast was missing from a map printed on napkins and displayed outside a popular Indian restaurant in Glasgow.The restaurant owners acknowledged the mistake and assured the Indian boxing contingent that it would be corrected.The incident took place when the Indian boxing team visited Mister Singh's India, The Home of Curry for a celebratory dinner after securing a record 10 medals, seven gold and three silver, at the Commonwealth Games.Lovlina noticed that the restaurant's branding showed an incomplete map of India without the Northeast. She immediately raised the issue with the management.Addressing the restaurant management during an interaction, Lovlina said the omission was upsetting."Please don't take this the wrong way. I felt a little hurt by this. In the map of India, our North East is missing. Yes, even outside, the map that's displayed has cut off the North East. As someone from the North East, that really hurts us. That's all I wanted to say.Please keep this in mind next time. Thank you so much," she said.Boxing Federation of India (BFI) president Ajay Singh, who was present at the restaurant, said there was no confrontation and that the issue was resolved amicably."There was no confrontation. It was an aberration and we pointed that out, me and Lovlina. They accepted their mistake and assured us that it will be corrected," Singh told PTI.The restaurant is a popular Indian dining destination in Glasgow and has hosted several visiting sports teams and dignitaries over the years.Lovlina won a silver medal in the women's 75kg boxing event at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.The Tokyo Olympic bronze medallist lost a closely fought final to Australia's Emma-Sue Greentree by a 4-1 split decision, missing out on her first Commonwealth Games gold medal.The silver was Lovlina's maiden Commonwealth Games medal after earlier exits at Gold Coast 2018 and Birmingham 2022.India's boxing team has produced its best-ever Commonwealth Games campaign, winning a record seven gold and three silver medals. Overall, India has collected 35 medals at the Glasgow Games: 11 gold, 16 silver and eight bronze to occupy fourth place in the medal standings.
Article Summary: Cwg silver medallist lovlina objects to'missing' northeast on glasgow restaurant's napkins. Incident took place when the indian boxing team visited mister singh's india, the home of curry for a celebratory dinner after securing a record 10 medals, seven gold and three silver.

Article Title: 'I gave up': Tejaswin Shankar's emotional confession after turning CWG heartbreak into historic bronze
Article Text:
Tejaswin Shankar celebrates after winning the bronze medal in the men's decathlon event. (PTI Photo)

'I questioned everything'

NEW DELHI: There were tears after one jump. Days later, there was history, a medal and a message that resonated far beyond the athletics track.Indian decathlete Tejaswin Shankar has opened up on the emotional turmoil he endured at the 2026 Commonwealth Games, revealing that he briefly "gave up" after a recurring knee injury shattered his hopes in the high jump before he picked himself up to script history with India's first-ever Commonwealth Games medal in the decathlon.The national record holder shared a deeply personal message on social media after returning home with a bronze medal, admitting the journey from heartbreak to the podium was one of the toughest tests of his career."There are moments in life when you feel like everything you've worked for is slipping away. This week, I had one of those moments," Tejaswin wrote.The 27-year-old had travelled to Glasgow hoping to defend the bronze medal he won in the high jump at the Birmingham Commonwealth Games in 2022 — India's first-ever medal in the event.Instead, his campaign unravelled almost instantly.A long-standing battle with chronic patellar tendinitis, commonly known as jumper's knee, resurfaced after his very first attempt in the high jump, forcing him to withdraw from the competition.The sight of Tejaswin crouching alone on the track, struggling to hold back tears, became one of the defining images of India's campaign.Those tears, however, were not because of physical pain."I’m going to be honest and admit for a while, I gave up," he revealed. "I questioned everything. I wondered if all the preparation had been for nothing."For any elite athlete, such moments can define a career. But for Tejaswin, they became the beginning of an extraordinary comeback.Instead of allowing disappointment to consume him, Tejaswin slowly rebuilt himself over the next few days."But somewhere along the way, I picked myself back up piece by piece. I was shattered emotionally but kept lying to myself that I was fine. One conversation, one treatment session, one event, one lap at a time," he added.Competing through pain, the Indian produced a remarkable performance across the gruelling two-day decathlon to finish with 7,976 points and claim the bronze medal — the first ever by an Indian in the event at the Commonwealth Games.It also marked his second Commonwealth Games medal after the high jump bronze in Birmingham four years ago.After clinching the historic podium finish, Tejaswin walked into the mixed zone with a smile replacing the tears seen earlier in the week."Guys, I won't cry today," he joked.The bronze was all the more remarkable considering he had entered the final 1,500m in third place and held on under immense physical and mental pressure to secure the medal.Reflecting on his remarkable turnaround, Tejaswin credited the people around him for helping him rediscover belief when he had lost faith in himself."Looking back, I realize I didn't do it alone. To my coaches, medical team, teammates, family, friends, sponsors, and every single person who called, messaged, or reached out on social media… thank you. Your belief carried me when I was struggling very hard to believe in myself," he wrote.The athlete also reflected on the deeper lessons sport continues to teach."Sport has a funny way of testing you. Sometimes it isn't about being the strongest or the most talented. Sometimes it's simply about refusing to stay down.""Proud to leave the Commonwealth Games with a bronze medal around my neck. It wasn't the path I imagined, but it taught me more than an easy victory ever could," he added.With Glasgow behind him, Tejaswin has already shifted his focus to the next challenge. Asian Games , see you soon. The Beast Never Stops," he concluded.
Article Summary: Indian decathlete tejaswin shankar has opened up on the emotional turmoil he endured at the 2026 commonwealth games. The 27-year-old revealed that he briefly "gave up" after a recurring knee injury shattered his hopes in the high jump. But he picked himself up to script history with india's first-ever commonwealth games medal in the decathlon.

Article Title: After historic CWG gold, Mirabai Chanu declares Asian Games 'make-or-break'
Article Text:
Mirabai Chanu (Image credit: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: There is little left for Saikhom Mirabai Chanu to conquer at the Commonwealth Games.A record-extending third consecutive CWG gold medal in Glasgow has only strengthened her status as the undisputed queen of Commonwealth weightlifting. Add the silver she won in her debut Games in 2014, and Mirabai now stands as the most successful weightlifting athlete in CWG history.Yet, less than 24 hours after standing atop the podium once again, the Tokyo Olympic silver medallist had already turned the page."The very next day after winning gold, I started preparing for the Asian Games . I started training the next day itself," Mirabai told TOI upon her return to India on Sunday afternoon.For the 32-year-old, the celebrations are over. The focus has shifted completely to the one medal that has remained painfully out of reach throughout her glittering career — an Asian Games podium finish."The upcoming Games in Japan are very important for me. I don't have an Asiad medal and I want to win one. Before every Asiad, I have either suffered an injury or something has happened because of which I missed out on a medal.This time I have to overcome that. My focus is purely on the event. That's the one title I desperately want to win," she said.Having carried Indian weightlifting on her shoulders for more than a decade while battling recurring injuries, Mirabai knows opportunities are becoming increasingly precious."I am not thinking whether this will be my last Asiad or not. But I will compete like this is the best opportunity I have to win a medal...like this is the only Asiad I have. Future competitions can wait. Right now, the Aich-Nagoya Games offers me the best chance. For me, it is a make-or-break moment."Those words carry the weight of a career shaped as much by injuries as medals.The build-up to Glasgow was anything but straightforward. Mirabai won gold at the National Championships in Modinagar in Feb, setting national records in the process, but picked up a shoulder injury during the competition. The setback forced her to miss the Asian Championships as she stepped away from competition for months to allow her body to recover.Her comeback, however, was vintage Mirabai.Competing in Glasgow after months away from the platform, she comfortably lifted a Games record total of 190kg — 85kg in snatch and 105kg in clean and jerk — to clinch India's first gold of this edition of the Games. More importantly, she achieved what no other weightlifter has managed before by winning three successive CWG gold.It was the performance of a champion who understood the bigger picture.Mirabai admitted she deliberately avoided exhausting herself in Glasgow, preserving both her body and energy for the much bigger challenge that awaits in Japan."I preserved myself during the CWG. My focus was always on the Asiad. Now I have to improve my performance level. The competition there will be much tougher."That challenge will be formidable. Olympic champion Hou Zhihui of China, the powerful North Korean lifters and Thailand's Surodchana Khambao are likely to headline a world-class field where every kilogram can separate the medal winners from the rest."I have to train harder. China, North Korea and Thailand have very strong weightlifters. I need to raise my performance several notches. I have to prepare more and train harder."Unlike previous major championships, Mirabai will remain in India for the final phase of her preparations under long-time coach Vijay Sharma."There isn't much time before the Games. We cannot go abroad now. I will train here in India under Vijay sir. I will follow the same routine as I do before every major championship. Nothing special, but my performance level has to improve."Years of competing at the highest level have also taught Mirabai to respect her body's limits."I understand my body much better now. I know how my mind and body react. I have learnt from injuries and experience. That understanding is very important."Beyond the Games lies another major transition. With the International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) scrapping the women's 49kg division for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Mirabai will eventually have to move up to the new 53kg category — another challenge in an already extraordinary career.But that is a story for another day. For now, India's most decorated Commonwealth weightlifter has only one destination in mind. "This Games is the biggest moment for me. I have to come back with a medal at any cost. I don't want to let this opportunity go."
Article Summary: Saikhom mirabai chanu won a record-extending third consecutive cwg gold medal in glasgow. The 32-year-old now stands as the most successful weightlifting athlete in cwg history. The tokyo olympic silver medallist had already turned the page. The international weightlifting federation (iwf) scrapping the women's 49kg division for the los angeles olympics in 2028.

Article Title: 'Vozinha! Vozinha!': FIFA World Cup breakout star gets hero's welcome in Chile after three delays
Article Text:
Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha arrives at the airport ahead of a move to Colo-Colo in Santiago, Chile. (AP Photo)

Three delays before dream move finally became reality



World Cup hero earns special jersey exception



Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

One of the biggest breakout stars of the 2026 FIFA World Cup has finally arrived in Chile — and the reception was nothing short of extraordinary.Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha, whose remarkable performances at the World Cup captured the imagination of football fans across the globe, landed in Santiago on Sunday to complete his move to Chilean giants Colo Colo after his arrival was delayed on three separate occasions.Hundreds of jubilant supporters gathered at Santiago's airport with flags, banners, drums and chants, turning the veteran goalkeeper's arrival into a celebration usually reserved for legends. Videos of the emotional welcome quickly spread across social media, underlining the popularity Vozinha has earned since his unforgettable World Cup campaign."I’m very happy to be here. And I want to thank the fans for the patience they’ve shown while waiting for me," the 40-year-old told reporters shortly after landing. "See you at the Monumental Stadium."Colo Colo, Chile's most successful football club, announced the signing of Josimar Évora Dias — better known worldwide as Vozinha — on July 24.However, what was expected to be a straightforward transfer soon became a complicated saga.Documentation issues and personal matters delayed the goalkeeper's arrival three different times, raising concerns among supporters eagerly waiting to welcome their new signing.The uncertainty finally ended on Sunday evening when Vozinha landed in Santiago at 8:35 p.m. local time to a rousing reception from hundreds of Colo Colo fans.The veteran is scheduled to undergo medical examinations before signing an initial six-month contract with an option to extend it by another year. He is expected to begin training with his new teammates on Tuesday before being officially unveiled by the club.Vozinha's move has already prompted an unprecedented rule change in Chilean football.The Chilean Football Federation unanimously voted to amend its regulations and allow the goalkeeper to wear "Vozinha" on the back of his jersey instead of his surname.Under previous league rules, players were required to display only their family names on their shirts.The exception reflects the global recognition attached to the nickname that became synonymous with Cape Verde's historic World Cup journey.Vozinha — whose nickname means "grandma" in Portuguese — became one of the tournament's most celebrated players after helping Cape Verde make history on their World Cup debut.At 40, he became the oldest player to feature in a nation's first-ever World Cup match and earned worldwide admiration with a string of spectacular saves against Spain, Uruguay and Argentina. His heroic display against eventual champions Spain, where he kept them scoreless, transformed him into one of the faces of the tournament.His popularity exploded during the competition. Before the World Cup, Vozinha had fewer than 50,000 Instagram followers. By the end of the tournament, that figure had soared beyond 29.5 million.For Colo Colo supporters, the excitement extends well beyond social media fame.Fans hope the experienced goalkeeper can inspire the Chilean league leaders to another domestic title before leading their challenge in next season's Copa Libertadores.
Article Summary: Three delays before dream move finally became reality for cape verde goalkeeper vozinha. The 40-year-old landed in santiago on sunday to complete his move to chilean giants colo colo. Hundreds of jubilant supporters gathered at santiago's airport with flags, banners, drums and chants.

Article Title: 18 years after Saina Nehwal, Tanvi Sharma brings Taipei Open title back to India
Article Text:
Tanvi Sharma (Image credit: BAI)

Dominant display in the final



Emotional moment with coach

Another milestone for the teenage star



Indian badminton player Tanvi Sharma won the first BWF World Tour title of her career after beating Vietnam's Thuy Linh Nguyen in the women's singles final of the Taipei Open Super 300 on Sunday.The 17-year-old from Punjab defeated the sixth seed 21-16, 21-16 in just 36 minutes to lift her maiden Super 300 trophy.Tanvi, who is coached by Park Tae-sang, the former coach of PV Sindhu, also became the first Indian woman to win the Taipei Open singles title since Saina Nehwal in 2008.Tanvi made an excellent start and used her clever drop shots and deceptive strokes to trouble Nguyen. She quickly raced to a 10-2 lead in the opening game.Although a few unforced errors allowed the Vietnamese player to reduce the gap, Tanvi regained control after the mid-game break. Strong smashes from both sides of the court helped her seal the first game 21-16.Nguyen started the second game better and moved 3-0 ahead, but Tanvi fought back to level the score at 3-3. She once again mixed powerful smashes with delicate net shots to take control of the rallies.The Indian gradually increased her lead to 15-10 and then 18-12.She earned seven match points and, despite missing three of them, finished the match with another winner to claim the biggest title of her career.After winning the title, Tanvi celebrated by taking off her gold medal and placing it around the neck of her coach Park Tae-sang. The two then posed together for photographs in a heartwarming moment.At 17 years and 222 days, Tanvi became the youngest finalist in the history of the Taipei Open, breaking the previous record held by Korean doubles legend Lee Yong Dae, who reached the men's doubles final in 2006 at 17 years and 287 days.Tanvi has enjoyed a rapid rise over the last two years. She became the first Indian to win two medals at a single World Junior Championships, claiming silver in girls' singles and bronze in the mixed team event.She was also part of the Indian team that won the country's first-ever gold medal at the Asian Team Championships.A former world junior No. 1, Tanvi had finished runner-up at the 2025 US Open Super 300, as well as the Odisha Masters Super 100 and Guwahati Masters Super 100, before finally winning her maiden BWF World Tour title in Taipei.
Article Summary: Tanvi sharma beat vietnam's thuy linh nguyen in the final of the taipei open super 300. The 17-year-old is coached by park tae-sang, the former coach of pv sindhu. Tanvi is the first indian woman to win the title since saina nehwal in 2008.

Article Title: 'I have a lot of respect for her': Pakistan's first female CWG boxing medallist credits Mary Kom for inspiring her
Article Text:
Mary Kom

Growing up in Pakistan's Punjab province, Fatima Zahra had few female boxing role models in her own country. She found one across the border in India's MC Mary Kom, whose journey inspired her to take up the sport and eventually become Pakistan's first female Commonwealth Games boxing medallist.The 22-year-old from Sargodha in Pakistan's Punjab province won a bronze medal in the women's 60kg event at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, becoming the first Pakistani woman boxer to stand on a Commonwealth Games podium.After her medal-winning campaign, Fatima said the person who inspired her to take up boxing was India's six-time world champion Mary Kom "I am inspired by India's Mary Kom," Fatima told news agency PTI after securing her bronze medal.Born into a poor farming family, Mary Kom overcame financial hardship, social resistance and limited resources to become one of the most successful boxers in history. She secretly trained in her early years while helping her family in the fields before winning six world championship titles, an Olympic bronze medal, Asian Games and Commonwealth Games gold medals, and five Asian Championships.Fatima said the 2014 Bollywood film based on Mary Kom's life became a source of motivation when she started boxing."I used to watch the film made on her life. When I started boxing I used to watch that movie and train. I have a lot of respect for her and inshallah one day I will become like her. I hope I can meet her," Fatima said.Like Mary Kom, Fatima also had to overcome opposition from her family before she could continue with boxing."My background is not that strong. My basic coach taught me everything," she said, as quotes by PTI."My family was against boxing. They would not let me go for training but I fought with them and continued training."She said her family's attitude has changed completely over the years."And now they are more tense than me for my fight and competition," she said with a smile.Fatima hopes her medal will encourage more girls in Pakistan to take up sport and follow their dreams."I was also just another girl. I joined boxing, trained and worked hard. I want other girls who are told to work at home to come out like me."
Article Summary: Fatima zahra is pakistan's first female commonwealth games boxing medallist. The 22-year-old won a bronze medal in the women's 60kg event in glasgow. Fatima said the person who inspired her to take up boxing was india's mary kom.

Article Title: Meet Nathan Thomas: 18-year-old Florida teen becomes the world's youngest male professor after breaking a 306-year-old record
Article Text:
How Nathan Thomas became the world's youngest male professor

Image: CBS Miami

An extraordinary academic journey

A passion for engineering and teaching

Looking beyond engineering





An inspiration for young learners

At an age when many students are just beginning university, Nathan Thomas had already stepped into the classroom as a college professor. The Florida native earned a place in the Guinness World Records after becoming the world's youngest male professor at just 18 years and 346 days old, breaking a record that had stood for 306 years. Thomas joined Miami Dade College as an engineering instructor, where he teaches students who are often close to his own age. His remarkable academic journey, which began with enrolling in college at the age of 10, has now made him one of the youngest educators ever to teach at the higher education level.Nathan Thomas officially became the world's youngest male professor when he accepted an engineering teaching position at Miami Dade College at the age of 18 years and 346 days. Guinness World Records confirmed that he surpassed the record previously held by Scottish mathematician Colin Maclaurin, who became a professor at the age of 19 in 1717. The achievement ended a record that had remained unbeaten for more than three centuries.Thomas began teaching COP 2270: C for Engineers at Miami Dade College in August 2023. The course introduces engineering students to the fundamentals of C programming and computational problem-solving.Many of his students are around the same age as him, but Thomas believes age matters far less than a willingness to learn. He has said that everyone enters the classroom with the same goal of gaining knowledge and improving their skills.Thomas displayed exceptional academic ability from an early age. At just 10 years old, he dual-enrolled at Miami Dade College while continuing his school education. By the age of 14, he had transferred to Florida International University, where he completed both bachelor's and master's degrees in electrical engineering with honours. His accelerated academic path eventually led him back to Miami Dade College, this time as a faculty member rather than a student.Coming from a family of engineers, Thomas developed an interest in mathematics and science at a young age. He has credited his mother with helping him understand mathematical concepts in ways that made learning enjoyable. He says the most rewarding part of teaching is watching students grasp ideas that once seemed difficult, describing those moments as just as satisfying as solving engineering problems himself.While continuing to teach, Thomas is also pursuing a Juris Doctor degree at the University of Miami School of Law, with an expected graduation in 2028. He hopes to combine his engineering background with legal expertise by specialising in intellectual property law, particularly in areas involving science, technology, engineering and mathematics. According to Thomas, the structured problem-solving skills he developed through engineering have proved valuable in his legal studies.Nathan Thomas's achievement demonstrates how determination, curiosity and a passion for learning can open extraordinary opportunities at a young age. From entering college as a child to becoming the world's youngest male professor and breaking a 306-year-old Guinness World Record, his journey has inspired students and educators alike. As he continues balancing teaching with law school, Thomas hopes to contribute to both education and innovation while encouraging others to pursue ambitious goals regardless of age.
Article Summary: Nathan thomas became the world's youngest male professor at 18 years and 346 days. He broke a record that had stood for 306 years. At just 10 years old, he dual-enrolled at miami dade college. He is also pursuing a juris doctor degree at the university of miami school of law.

Article Title: ​From cancer survivors to surfing stars: California woman and her dog beat cancer before competing together at the World Dog Surfing Championships
Article Text:
Image credit: AP

From cancer survivors to world championship surfers

Rusty's surfing talent began as a puppy

Making waves at the World Dog Surfing Championships

What is the World Dog Surfing Championships?

More than a competition

A story that touched hearts

A California woman and her beloved Miniature Pinscher have become an inspiration after overcoming one of life's toughest challenges and returning to do what they love most together. Sophia Sadlowski, from Huntington Beach, California, and her dog Rusty, both survived cancer before competing side by side at the 2026 World Dog Surfing Championships held at Linda Mar Beach in Pacifica, California. Although they did not win the competition, their remarkable journey captured the hearts of spectators and highlighted the extraordinary bond between humans and their pets. Their appearance proved that resilience, determination and companionship can be just as memorable as standing on the winners' podium.Sophia Sadlowski and Rusty share a story that extends far beyond surfing. Both battled cancer and successfully recovered before returning to the sport they enjoy together. While Sadlowski has not publicly disclosed the specific types of cancer they faced, she confirmed that both she and Rusty are now cancer-free. Their participation at the championships served as a celebration of recovery and hope, inspiring fellow competitors and spectators alike.Rusty's surfing career started unexpectedly when Sadlowski placed him on a surfboard as a young puppy simply to take a photograph. Instead of jumping off, the Miniature Pinscher balanced himself with ease and rode a wave back to shore. Recognising his natural ability, Sadlowski continued training with him, and Rusty entered his first surfing competition at just four months old. He impressed judges by finishing third in his debut event, marking the beginning of an unusual sporting partnership.The duo competed together at the 10th World Dog Surfing Championships, held on August 1, 2026, at Linda Mar Beach in Pacifica, California. Rusty wore a green life jacket complete with a playful shark fin and protective dog goggles as he rode the waves alongside Sadlowski on the same surfboard. Their performance drew loud cheers from beachgoers, not only because of Rusty's surfing skills but also because of the inspiring journey that brought them to the event.The World Dog Surfing Championships were first held in 2016 and have since become one of the world's most unique canine sporting events. Dogs compete in categories based on their size, while additional tandem events allow multiple dogs or dogs and their owners to surf together. Judges assess competitors on factors including balance, confidence, ride duration, wave quality and overall style, rewarding dogs that demonstrate control and composure on the water.The annual event is designed to support animal welfare alongside competitive surfing. It raises funds for animal charities and rescue organisations while hosting pet adoption drives, educational activities and family-friendly entertainment. The championships encourage responsible pet ownership and celebrate the close relationship between people and their dogs, making the event about much more than trophies and rankings.Although Sophia Sadlowski and Rusty did not claim the championship title, they emerged as two of the event's most memorable participants. Their story reminded spectators that some victories cannot be measured by medals or podium finishes. After overcoming cancer together, simply standing on the same surfboard and sharing the waves represented a powerful triumph. Their journey from survivors to competitors continues to inspire people and demonstrates the resilience, trust and companionship that can exist between a person and their dog.
Article Summary: Sophia sadlowski, from huntington beach, california, and her dog rusty, both survived cancer before competing side by side at the 2026 world dog surfing championships. Although they did not win the competition, their remarkable journey captured the hearts of spectators and highlighted the extraordinary bond between humans and their pets.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jim Brown: "I set my standards so high, no one could be harsher on me than…" - a simple philosophy behind extraordinary success and discipline
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jim Brown (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Jim Brown

"I set my standards so high, no one could be harsher on me than I was"

Understand the meaning behind Jim Brown’s quote

Where this quote actually comes from

Why personal standards matter more than public opinion

Why real accountability starts with yourself first

Why discipline produces consistency that motivation alone cannot

Why the goal was never actually perfection

Why criticism gets easier to handle once real standards exist

Why this idea clearly reaches beyond sport entirely

A note on Jim Brown's legacy

Other famous quotes by Jim Brown

"There were a lot of running backs as good as me. The real difference was that I could focus. I never laid back and relied on natural ability."

"The power is between your ears. The power is in your heart."

"I don't teach kids to be number 1. What I teach is to be as good as you can be. Use what you have and be as good as you can be. That's all you can do, anyway."

"You can't get old without living."

Why this quote is relevant

Success often gets credited to talent, opportunity or simple luck. Jim Brown , widely regarded as one of the greatest American football players in history, pointed somewhere else entirely. "I set my standards so high, no one could be harsher on me than I was," he said. His toughest critic was never an opposing team or someone in the media. It was his own expectation of himself, set high enough that outside judgment genuinely could not compete with it, a discipline that carried him through nine remarkable seasons in the NFL and continued shaping how he lived the rest of his life afterwards.Brown is describing where his real accountability actually came from. He was not relying on coaches, critics or public opinion to push him harder than he already pushed himself. He had already set personal standards demanding enough that no outside judgement could realistically exceed them. This reflects genuine self-discipline, not self-punishment. It encourages people to chase real improvement by focusing on their own growth rather than constantly seeking approval from someone else.This line is documented in Out of Bounds, Brown's 1990 memoir written with Steve Delsohn, published by Kensington Publishing Corporation. Brown has also spoken directly about what actually separated him from other talented runners of his era. "There were a lot of running backs as good as me," he said. "The real difference was that I could focus. I never laid back and relied on natural ability." That is really the same idea from today's quote, stated from a slightly different angle.People often spend a huge amount of energy worrying about what other people think of them. Feedback genuinely has value, but relying entirely on outside validation tends to limit someone rather than help them. People with strong personal standards evaluate their own work honestly, regardless of whether praise or criticism happens to be coming their way at the time. Their motivation comes from actually doing their best, not from impressing anyone watching.Blaming circumstances is always the easier option when something goes wrong. People who genuinely succeed over the long run tend to ask a different question instead, what could I have actually done better here. Taking that kind of responsibility does not mean expecting perfection from yourself. It means recognising that real improvement starts with honest self-reflection, focused specifically on whatever you can actually control.Motivation rises and falls depending on the day. Discipline stays in place regardless. High personal standards keep effort consistent even once the initial enthusiasm has faded. Brown became one of the greatest players in the sport not purely through natural ability, but because he approached his own preparation with real, sustained commitment, exactly the trait he describes in his own words above.None of this should be read as demanding literal perfection. Nobody performs flawlessly every single time, and Brown himself never claimed otherwise. What his quote really reflects is a commitment to continuous improvement, using high standards to encourage genuine growth rather than fear. The actual goal was becoming better than yesterday, not becoming flawless overnight.People with strong internal standards tend to be less shaken by outside criticism. Constructive feedback starts to function as useful information rather than a personal attack, since they have already examined their own performance honestly before anyone else even weighs in. Confidence tends to grow once self-evaluation actually matters more than public judgement.Brown's underlying philosophy applies just as well outside football. Students working toward academic excellence, entrepreneurs building a business from scratch, scientists chasing a genuine discovery, artists refining their own craft. In every field, long-term success tends to depend less on outside pressure and more on a genuine personal commitment to keep improving.Jim Brown, who lived from 1936 to 2023, is widely regarded as one of the greatest running backs in the history of American football. Across nine seasons with the Cleveland Browns, he led the league in rushing multiple times and was named the NFL's Most Valuable Player on several occasions. He retired from football at the peak of his career to pursue acting, and later devoted much of his life to community programmes and social advocacy.Brown's words are a reminder that real excellence rarely comes from fear of criticism. It grows out of the discipline to hold yourself accountable even when nobody else is actually watching. People who genuinely maintain high personal standards keep learning and improving regardless of whether outside recognition ever arrives at all. The standards someone chooses for themselves, far more than the world's judgement of their achievements, are usually what end up shaping their actual character and the legacy they eventually leave behind.
Article Summary: Quote of the day by jim brown: "i set my standards so high, no one could be harsher on me than i was" brown is widely regarded as one of the greatest american football players in history. The quote reflects a commitment to continuous improvement. Jim brown is widely regarded as one of the greatest running backs in the history of american football.

Article Title: Quote of the day by LeBron James: "I think the reason why I'm the person who I am today is because…" - an inspiring lesson on resilience, adversity and the power of difficult beginnings
Article Text:
Quote of the day by LeBron James (AP photo)

Quote of the day by LeBron James

"I think the reason why I'm the person who I am today is because I went through those tough times when I was younger"

What is the meaning behind the quote by LeBron James

The real story behind this quote

Why difficulty can genuinely build strength

Why where someone starts does not have to decide where they end up

Why resilience keeps growing through actual experience

Why gratitude often follows real struggle

Why real success tends to carry a real responsibility with it

Why this idea clearly reaches well beyond basketball

Other memorable quotes by LeBron James

"Nothing is given. Everything is earned."

"You can't be afraid to fail. It's the only way you succeed."

"Commitment is a big part of what I am and what I believe."

"Don't be afraid of failure. This is the way to succeed."

Why this quote matters today

Success stories usually get told through trophies and record books, with the years of actual struggle quietly left out of the story. LeBron James refuses to leave his out. "I think the reason why I'm the person who I am today is because I went through those tough times when I was younger," he said. Rather than wishing his difficult childhood had simply not happened, he treats it as the actual foundation everything else was built on, a perspective that has shaped how he talks about his own career and his life away from basketball just as much as anything he ever did on the court.LeBron is acknowledging directly that his difficult childhood genuinely shaped who he became, rather than something he simply had to overcome and forget about afterwards. He is not celebrating hardship for its own sake. He is recognising that difficult experiences taught him things he might never have learned any other way, patience, gratitude, and a determination that comfortable circumstances rarely produce on their own.LeBron grew up in Akron, Ohio, and has spoken directly about how unstable his early years actually were. "When I was 5, some financial things happened, and I moved seven times in a year," he said."We moved from apartment to apartment, sometimes living with friends. My mom would always say, 'don't get comfortable, because we might not be here long.'" He was raised largely by his mother, Gloria James, and has also said that being the only man in the household with her helped him grow up fast. He later described himself plainly, capturing exactly how unlikely his own path had actually been: "I'm LeBron James, from Akron, Ohio, from the inner city. I'm not even supposed to be here."Life rarely follows a smooth, predictable path for anyone, however talented or driven they turn out to be later on. People run into setbacks, disappointments and challenges they never planned for. Painful as it usually is in the moment, that kind of adversity also tends to build real resilience. People who learn to get through genuinely hard periods often end up far more confident about handling whatever comes next, and LeBron's own career is a fairly direct illustration of exactly that pattern.Plenty of people quietly assume their circumstances at the start of life more or less decide how the rest of it will go. LeBron's own story argues against that directly. Despite a genuinely difficult childhood, he became one of the greatest basketball players in history, while also building schools, supporting entire communities, and becoming a serious entrepreneur along the way. Where someone begins clearly shapes them. It was never really the same thing as locking them in permanently.Confidence does not only come from winning. It also builds through simply surviving something genuinely difficult, at a time when nobody would have blamed a person for giving up entirely. Every genuine challenge that gets overcome becomes real evidence that the next one is survivable too. People who have already made it through real hardship tend to carry a quieter, steadier kind of confidence, precisely because they already know firsthand that they can handle it.People who have actually lived through hardship tend to appreciate opportunities that others might take for granted without a second thought. LeBron has spoken often about valuing family, education, and giving back to the community he came from, and that instinct clearly traces back directly to his own early circumstances. Gratitude tends to run deeper once someone genuinely remembers how far they have actually come.LeBron has used his own platform repeatedly to support education and community development, most notably through the I PROMISE School he helped establish in Akron, which serves at-risk children from the same kind of background he grew up in himself. His quote suggests that personal success was never really only about individual achievement. It also opens up genuine opportunities to help other people facing the exact same struggles he once faced himself.Although LeBron is speaking specifically from his own experience in sport, the same lesson applies everywhere. Students working through genuinely difficult circumstances, entrepreneurs rebuilding after a real failure, professionals starting out with very limited resources, parents working hard simply to give their own children a better shot than they had. Every real challenge carries some potential to build strength that eventually gets used later.LeBron's quote is a reminder that success is rarely built purely on comfort. The challenges someone actually lives through tend to shape their character more deeply than their easy wins ever could, teaching a kind of resilience and perspective that comfortable circumstances simply do not require. A difficult beginning was never really a life sentence. With enough perseverance, patience and a willingness to keep working through it, it can become the actual foundation for something considerably bigger than anyone watching from the outside would have guessed.
Article Summary: "i think the reason why i'm the person who i am today is because i went through those tough times when i was younger" - lebron james. Lebron grew up in akron, ohio, and has spoken directly about how unstable his early years actually were. He is acknowledging directly that his difficult childhood shaped who he became.

Article Title: Prince William and Kate Middleton make rare family appearance with Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis at Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow
Article Text:
Prince William and Kate Middleton make rare family appearance with Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis at Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow

Rare royal family outing during summer break

Charlotte's Commonwealth Games connection

Other royals also attended Glasgow Games

Prince William and Kate Middleton briefly paused their summer break to attend the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, on Saturday, August 1, making it a rare family outing with their three children - Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis.The Prince and Princess of Wales, both 44, were joined by Prince George, 13, Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8, for the sporting event. According to reports by The Telegraph and GB News, the appearance marked the siblings' first official public engagement in Scotland.Known as the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland, William and Kate spent time meeting Team Wales athletes and their families during the Games. The royal couple also visited SportsAid, the youth sports charity of which Kate has served as patron since 2013, highlighting its work in supporting promising young athletes.The Wales family typically keeps a low profile during the summer holidays, using the school break to spend private time together. They are also expected to spend part of the season at Balmoral Castle, where the British royal family traditionally gathers in late summer.Although Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis are largely kept out of the public eye, they occasionally accompany their parents to major public events.Earlier this summer, George and Charlotte joined William and Kate at the Wimbledon men's singles final, where they watched Italy's Jannik Sinner successfully defend his title against Germany's Alexander Zverev. Princess Kate later presented the trophies in her role as patron of the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club. Prince Louis did not attend the Wimbledon outing.This was not Princess Charlotte's first Commonwealth Games appearance. The revised edition featured athletes from all 74 Commonwealth nations competing across 10 sports, including athletics, swimming, gymnastics, boxing, netball, judo and weightlifting, with several disciplines also featuring adaptive sports competitions.King Charles III and Queen Camilla officially opened the Games on July 23 with a memorable entrance from the iconic Doctor Who TARDIS prop at Glasgow's Hydro Stadium. Article Title: Quote of the day by Tiger Woods: "Talent is something you are born with, and a skill is something you…" - a lesson on why practice matters more than natural ability
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Tiger Woods (Getty Images)

Quote of the day by Tiger Woods

The deeper meaning of Tiger Wood’s quote

Why Woods himself is the perfect person to say this

Why skill keeps growing while talent stays roughly where it started

Why consistent practice tends to beat raw potential

Why repeating the basics is what actually builds mastery

Why mistakes end up teaching more than easy wins do

Why discipline tends to matter more than motivation

Other famous quotes by Tiger Woods

"No matter how good you get you can always get better, and that's the exciting part."

"Achievements on the golf course are not what matters, decency and honesty are what matter."

"Other golfers may outplay me from time to time, but they'll never outwork me."

"We all make decisions. But in the end, our decisions make us."

Why this quote is relevant

Watching a champion perform can make success look effortless, as though it were simply handed to a lucky few at birth. Tiger Woods pushed back on that idea directly. "Talent is something you are born with, and a skill is something you develop," he said. "99% of what you need to succeed in golf are skills." Talent might give someone a starting point. What actually determines how far they get is what they choose to practise and refine every single day after that, a lesson that Woods himself spent decades proving through his own extraordinarily disciplined career. What gives this quote unusual weight is that Woods didn't just say it once and move on. He proved it repeatedly, rebuilding his swing and his body after injury after injury, when relying purely on natural gift would have quietly ended his career years earlier. His comeback victory at the 2019 Masters, after years of injury and self-doubt, stands as perhaps the clearest proof yet that patient, deliberate skill-building can outlast even the harshest setbacks any career throws at it. His words remind us that while talent may open the door, it is disciplined practice, resilience and continuous improvement that ultimately determine lasting success."Talent is something you are born with, and a skill is something you develop. 99% of what you need to succeed in golf are skills"Woods draws a clear line between two very different things.Talent is natural ability, something someone may already have from a young age. Skill is something earned, built up through repetition, discipline, learning from mistakes and steady, continuous improvement, none of which arrives automatically no matter how talented someone started out. Saying that 99% of golfing success comes from skill is Woods arguing that raw natural ability, on its own, is almost never enough. Even the most naturally gifted players still need thousands of hours refining the basics and correcting weaknesses. The quote shifts attention away from what someone was simply born with and toward what they can actually control through effort.Woods has been blunt about his own background in the past. "People don't understand that when I grew up, I was never the most talented," he said. "I was never the biggest. I was never the fastest. I certainly was never the strongest. The only thing I had was my work ethic, and that's been what has gotten me this far." That is not a modest exaggeration. It is exactly the same claim the main quote is making, just told from the inside.Across a career spanning decades, Woods has won 15 major championships and 82 PGA Tour events, a total that ties him for the most wins in PGA Tour history. His success was never built on natural ability alone.
